title: Dearborn Mayor Explains Record Voter Turnout in Abdul El-Sayed Senate Election
content: NPR host Leila Fadel interviewed Abdullah Hammoud, mayor of Dearborn, Michigan, about why the city saw a record turnout in the election that sent Abdul El‑Sayed to the U.S. Senate.
summary: NPR host Leila Fadel speaks with Abdullah Hammoud, the mayor of Dearborn, Michigan, about why his city turned out in record numbers to elect Abdul El-Sayed to the U. S.
author: NPR Politics

title: Delhi braces for pollution season as smog pushes AQI above 650
content: Delhi is preparing for a “pollution season” as dense smog envelops the capital. The city’s air quality index has already risen above 650, exceeding the World Health Organization’s safe limit by more than 30 times.
summary: Delhi is bracing for a “pollution season” as smog covers the city. The air quality index has risen above 650, more than 30 times the World Health Organization’s safe limit.
author: Guardian Environment

title: 43 pilot whales die in mass stranding on New Zealand's Ngawi coast
content: More than 40 pilot whales died after a mass stranding on New Zealand’s remote east coast. Conservation officials reported that 43 whales were found dead along the Ngawi coast on the south‑eastern tip of the North Island. Volunteers and conservation workers attempted to rescue the beached animals, but rescuers were unable to save them on the rocky, isolated shoreline. The Department of Conservation confirmed the death toll and the location of the stranding.
summary: More than 40 pilot whales died after a mass stranding on New Zealand's remote east coast. The Department of Conservation said 43 whales had died along the Ngawi coast on the south‑eastern tip of the North Island.
author: Guardian Environment

title: UK trees show early spring six months ahead as autumn temperatures stay above average
content: UK trees are flowering about six months early, an “early spring” attributed to unusually mild autumn temperatures. Experts say the premature blooming could pose long‑term risks for pollinators. October was warmer than average across the UK, marking the ninth consecutive month of above‑average mean temperatures.
summary: Trees in the UK are experiencing an “early spring” with flowering occurring six months early because autumn temperatures have been mild. Experts warn that the unusually warm October, the ninth consecutive month above average, could cause long‑term harm to pollinators.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study finds clinical traits linked to brain network connectivity in consciousness disorders
content:
A new study published in The Innovation Life reports a link between clinical characteristics and brain network connectivity in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). Researchers from the Institute of Biophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing Tiantan Hospital and Capital Medical University found that factors such as etiology, age and time since injury are associated with patterns of brain connectivity.

The authors note that these clinical characteristics influence functional recovery, highlighting their importance in predicting outcomes for DoC patients, whose recovery has been difficult to forecast because of diverse injury causes and demographic backgrounds.
summary: Study finds clinical traits linked to brain network connectivity in consciousness disorders.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Astrocytes aid sustained brain activity and blood flow during prolonged sensory stimulation
content: New research shows that astrocytes—star‑shaped non‑neuronal cells—play an active role in sustaining both brain activity and blood flow when sensory stimulation persists for extended periods, such as during jogging, reading or listening to music. The study confirms that ongoing sensory input continuously activates specific neuronal groups, raising their demand for oxygen and nutrients, which in turn triggers dilation of nearby blood vessels through neurovascular coupling. While astrocytes have long been suspected of contributing to this process, the findings clarify how they help maintain the heightened neuronal and vascular response during prolonged stimulation.
summary: Prolonged sensory stimulation activates specific neuron groups, raising their oxygen and nutrient demand and triggering blood‑vessel dilation through neurovascular coupling. Astrocytes are shown to help sustain the resulting brain activity and blood flow, though their precise contribution has been unclear.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nasal spray combination shows relief for chronic blockage without rebound congestion in early trial
content:
Blocked noses can interfere with sleep and diminish the taste of food, becoming increasingly frustrating over time. Traditional nasal decongestant sprays, such as oxymetazoline, offer quick relief but may worsen obstruction when used repeatedly, producing irritation and inflammation in the nasal passages.

A recent early‑stage clinical trial sought a different approach. Researchers tested a combination of drugs designed to provide sustained relief from chronic nasal blockage without the rebound congestion that often follows overuse of standard decongestants.

The study’s goal was to identify a nasal spray duo that alleviates stubborn congestion while avoiding the rebound effect, potentially offering a more reliable solution for people who struggle with persistent nasal obstruction.
summary: An early clinical trial evaluated a drug combination intended to relieve chronic nasal blockage without causing rebound congestion. The duo was reported to provide lasting relief while avoiding the irritation and inflammation linked to overuse of decongestant sprays such as oxymetazoline.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Jesús de Miguel dies in CD Tenerife vs FC Andorra match, possible commotio cordis
content:
A player for CD Tenerife, Jesús de Miguel, died during a Spanish Segunda División match against FC Andorra. No official statement has confirmed the cause of his death, but some reports have suggested it may have been commotio cordis.  

Commotio cordis is described as a rare but well‑known medical condition that can trigger sudden cardiac arrest when a blow strikes the chest. The incident has prompted attention to this potential cause of fatal injury in contact sports.
summary: Jesús de Miguel, a CD Tenerife player, died after a Spanish Segunda División match against FC Andorra. Although no official cause has been confirmed, some reports say the death may have been due to commotio cordis, a rare condition that can cause sudden cardiac arrest after a chest blow.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Macrophage 'gatekeeper' cells limit stem-like T cell entry into tumors, study finds
content:
A new study led by King's College London, published in Cell Stem Cell, shows that chemotherapy can attract a specific population of immune cells—stem‑like T cells—to tumors.  

The researchers discovered that macrophages surrounding tumor blood vessels act as a barrier, limiting the stem‑like T cells’ ability to enter. By blocking the enzyme heme oxygenase‑1 (HO‑1) in these macrophages, the barrier was reduced, allowing more stem‑like T cells to infiltrate the tumor and contribute to an antitumor immune response.
summary: A new study led by King's College London has found that chemotherapy helps attract a specific population of immune cells called stem-like T cells toward tumors. The research, published in Cell Stem Cell, found that macrophages around tumor blood vessels can act as a barrier, limiting the T cells' ability to enter.
author: Medical Xpress

title: McGill researchers develop putty-like electrode to aid vocal rehabilitation
content: A team of researchers at McGill University has created a putty‑like electrode that conforms to the skin, aiming to enhance treatment and monitoring of voice disorders and upper‑airway diseases. In a proof‑of‑concept test, the sensor performed comparably to a standard clinical electrode in noise level, stability and in recording activity from small neck muscles.
summary: A team of McGill University researchers has developed a putty-like electrode that molds to the skin to improve treatment and monitoring of voice disorders and upper airway diseases. In a proof-of-concept study, the sensor matched a standard clinical electrode for noise and stability while recording activity from small neck muscles.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Australian children in poorer areas fall behind in psychological care, study says
content: Australian children from poorer communities are increasingly missing out on psychological care, according to research from Monash University. The study finds that the gap in treatment between wealthy and disadvantaged families has widened substantially over the past decade, leaving children in low‑income areas hardest hit.
summary: Australian children from poorer communities are increasingly missing out on psychological care. Monash University research finds the gap in treatment between wealthy and disadvantaged families has widened substantially over the past decade.
author: Medical Xpress

title: UNEP Report Warns Adaptation Finance Falls Short as Global Warming Exceeds 1.5°C
content: The United Nations Environment Programme reports that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 °C. The agency’s new study finds adaptation finance far short of what is needed, implementation hindered by institutional barriers, and mounting losses and damages.
summary: A new UNEP report says adaptation finance is far short of what is needed as global warming is set to exceed 1.5°C. The report also notes that implementation is constrained by institutional barriers and that losses and damages are mounting.
author: Phys.org

title: ACF report links Australian deforestation to beef farming and bank loans
content: ACF's latest report, "Bulldozers and Broken Promises," an investigation into deforestation, has ruffled a few feathers. But someone has to do it. Why? Because deforestation is a huge problem in Australia.
summary: ACF's latest report "Bulldozers and Broken Promises" investigates deforestation in Australia. The investigation links Australian deforestation to beef farming and major bank loans.
author: Phys.org

title: Indian engineer Mudasir Ali builds online wildlife alert after mother’s bear death
content: After his mother was killed in a bear attack in Kashmir, Indian software engineer Mudasir Ali created an online early‑warning system to help residents of the Himalayan region avoid dangerous wildlife encounters. The system alerts users to potential bear activity.
summary: Mudasir Ali, an Indian software engineer, created an online early‑warning system for wildlife. He built it after his mother was killed in a bear attack in Kashmir to help people in the Himalayan region avoid dangerous encounters.
author: Phys.org

title: Cancer-linked gene uses shortcut to trigger cell division
content: A cancer‑linked gene has been reported to use a “shortcut” to trigger cell division, underscoring the importance of tightly regulated replication for proper tissue development and recovery from injury. Uncontrolled cell division can lead to cancer, highlighting why timing of division is essential.
summary: A cancer-linked gene uses a shortcut to trigger cell division. Unregulated replication of living cells can lead to problems like cancer.
author: Phys.org

title: International scientists propose AI roadmap to advance ecosystem understanding
content: An international team of scientists has presented a roadmap describing how a new generation of artificial‑intelligence models could reshape ecological research. The outlined approach aims to enhance understanding of ecosystems and improve predictions of how they will respond to environmental change.
summary: An international team of scientists has outlined a roadmap for using new artificial intelligence models in ecology. They say the models could transform understanding of ecosystems and help predict responses to environmental change.
author: Phys.org

title: High-elevation terraces indicate faster uplift in Italy's Siculo-Calabrian rift zone
content: High‑elevation terraces in southern Italy indicate faster‑than‑expected uplift, according to new research by University of Oregon geologist Becky Dorsey. Her study focuses on the Siculo‑Calabrian rift zone, a fault belt extending over 100 miles (160 km). The data may improve earthquake hazard assessment in this seismically active region.
summary: University of Oregon geologist Becky Dorsey's latest research sheds light on the Siculo-Calabrian rift zone, a belt of faults spanning more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) in southern Italy. The new data could help improve earthquake hazard assessment in this seismically active region.
author: Phys.org

title: New metric quantifies risk across all carbon removal projects
content: A new standardized metric now allows the risk of uncertain carbon‑removal projects to be quantified. The metric can be applied across all schemes, whether involving forests, underground storage or other technologies, providing a common basis for comparing their risk profiles.
summary: A new standardized metric can quantify the risk of carbon removal projects. The metric can be applied across all schemes regardless of the technology used.
author: Phys.org

title: NASA to send robot GIMLI to explore lunar cave for future moon base
content: A robot named GIMLI is slated to explore a lunar cave as part of preparations for a future moon base. NASA is planning to send the cave‑hunting robot ahead of human crews, a development highlighted by columnist Robin George Andrews amid a growing race to build a lunar settlement.
summary: A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave as part of preparations for a future moon base. Columnist Robin George Andrews reports that NASA is sending the cave‑hunting robot ahead of humans.
author: New Scientist

title: Stonehenge altar origin still unknown as north‑east Scotland source dismissed
content:
Geologists are getting closer to solving the mystery as tests suggest the altar stone at Stonehenge may have come from elsewhere in Scotland, northern England, or Ireland.  

They spent countless hours on weather‑battered Scottish hills searching for the stone’s origin, but a new scientific report reveals the origin remains elusive and the north‑east Scotland theory has been ruled out.  

The report also suggests the geologists may have been looking in the wrong spot.
summary: Geologists report that tests indicate the altar stone may have come from other parts of Scotland, northern England or Ireland, ruling out a north‑east Scotland source. A new scientific report says the stone’s provenance remains elusive despite extensive fieldwork on Scottish hills.
author: Guardian Science

title: ISS Astronaut Captures Utah Goosenecks State Park in Stunning Space Photo
content:
Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks

The San Juan River, which now empties into Lake Powell, once behaved much like the modern Mississippi River. Tens of millions of years ago it flowed across a flat plain that had formed in an ancient marine environment. Because the terrain was smooth, the river meandered slowly and gently. When the Colorado Plateau began to rise about 20 million years ago, the river’s headwaters were lifted, increasing its gradient and speed. The resulting erosive power carved deeper, more dramatic curves into the 300‑million‑year‑old rock that now forms Utah’s Goosenecks State Park.

Today the San Juan cuts through a canyon roughly 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep. Its entrenched meanders—known locally as “goosenecks”—create horseshoe‑shaped bends that can be almost circular. In one particularly winding section the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—or goose—flies. The park’s dramatic topography was captured by an astronaut aboard the International Space Station on October 6, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera set to a 400‑millimeter focal length. The image, taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew, was later cropped, enhanced for contrast, and had lens artifacts removed. It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center and is freely available online.

Goosenecks State Park is not only a geological marvel but also a premier dark‑sky destination. The park earned an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. Its remote, high‑desert setting and 360‑degree views allow observers to see the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud in the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way with the unaided eye. In November 2026 the dark skies will host the peaks of the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids meteor showers.

The NASA Earth Observatory article, written by Lindsey Doermann, includes references to the DarkSky International designation, the tectonic history of the Colorado Plateau, and earlier Earth‑observing images of the Mississippi River. Additional astronaut photographs can be accessed through the NASA/JSC Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth.
summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed Utah’s Goosenecks State Park on October 6, 2026, capturing the 1,000‑foot deep canyon where the San Juan River carves its winding meanders. The park, designated an International Dark Sky Park in 2021, offers spectacular night views and hosts meteor showers in November 2026.
author: NASA News

title: NASA’s Swift Observatory Reenters Over Indonesia After 22 Years
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 6 – A… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Farewell to Swift Explanation: It is time to say goodbye to NASA ‘s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. After nearly 22 years of service, the satellite re-entered Earth’s atmosphere on November 4 at 7:39 EST over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia. The featured image is a mosaic created in 2018 using the first one million images captured by the satellite’s Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope. Swift had a combination of instruments, including an X-ray telescope and a gamma-ray telescope, that worked together to enable humanity to study, in unprecedented detail, the fastest and most energetic explosions in the universe. The most recent solar maximum accelerated the decay of the satellite’s orbit. An innovative mission to rescue Swift by boosting its orbit was not successful. Swift burned on reentry like a shooting star, but the impressive data acquired by the telescope over its mission will continue to bring light to the mysteries of the cosmos for years to come. May it keep inspiring new missions to boldly go into space, explore new data and seek out new science. Tomorrow’s picture: what’s next? Date November 6, 2026 Credit NASA / Swift and AndreaMosaic Authors & editors: Cecilia Chirenti, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Keighley Rockcliffe A service of: ASD at NASA / GSFC, NASA Science Activation & Michigan Tech. U. Random APOD Generator Yesterday’s Image APOD: 2026 November 5 – Enceladus in Silhouette Tomorrow’s Image
summary: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re‑entered Earth’s atmosphere on 4 November at 7:39 EST, burning over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia after nearly 22 years in service. The APOD image for 6 November 2026 is a 2018 mosaic of the first one million ultraviolet/optical telescope images, commemorating the satellite’s mission.
author: NASA News

title: Tau Robotics' remotely piloted humanoid robot cleans San Francisco apartment
content: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself. But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said. Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger. In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle. The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out. Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI. But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care. Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.
summary: Tau Robotics deployed a four‑and‑a‑half‑foot humanoid robot to a San Francisco apartment, with human operators controlling it via cameras mounted in its head and wrists. During the hour‑long visit the robot cleaned the kitchen and toilet, struggled with the building’s stairs and occasional overheating, and needed staff assistance to complete the job.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Greenlight Family Hub Digital Wall Calendar on sale before Black Friday
content: The Greenlight Family Hub is a digital wall calendar that displays family schedules, manages children’s chores, and functions as a photo frame. The device is currently offered at a discounted price in advance of the upcoming Black Friday sale.
summary: The Greenlight Family Hub displays your family calendars, manages your kid’s chores, and doubles as a photo frame. It is already discounted ahead of Black Friday.
author: Wired

title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production at Texas Gigafactory mid‑next year
content:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced on X that the company will “wind down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around the middle of next year. The pause is intended to free capacity for increased Cybercab (robotaxi) output. The Austin, Texas plant is currently the only Tesla facility known to assemble the Cybertruck and is equipped to produce its specialized components.

Musk did not say whether Cybertruck manufacturing will be shifted to another location, noting that moving production would be difficult.
summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on X the company will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around the middle of next year. The change is meant to make room for increased Cybercab production, and Musk did not say if production will be moved elsewhere.
author: The Verge

title: Russia and US aim to block UN proposal for binding autonomous weapons rules
content:
UN conference this month is seen as a key moment after years of discussions on filling a gap in the governance of AI systems. Plans to fill a gap in global governance of autonomous weapons are in jeopardy as a group of nations led by Russia and the US moves to use the conference to block proposals for a legally binding set of rules.

The scale of opposition will become clear at a diplomatic retreat starting on Friday ahead of the seventh review conference on “certain conventional weapons” in Geneva, which is expected to be attended by 128 countries from 16 to 20 November.
summary: Russia and US aim to block UN proposal for binding autonomous weapons rules.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Google, Meta, TikTok sue California to block child‑addiction social media law
content: Law bans social media platforms from providing minors features such as autoplay that lead to compulsive use Google, Meta and TikTok have sued California to block enforcement of ⁠a new state law intended ⁠to limit the risk ​of addicting children under 16 to social media platforms. The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits such platforms from offering underage children “psychologically exploitative features” that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing ⁠personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children’s accounts with those features.
summary: Google, Meta and TikTok have sued California to block enforcement of Assembly Bill 1709, a law that bans platforms from providing under‑16 users features such as autoplay that could lead to compulsive use. The law also requires deletion of children’s accounts that have those features.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Trump weighs Iran strike as Ukraine talks head to Abu Dhabi
content: After the U.S. midterms, focus shifts to Donald Trump’s potential next action on Iran, with U.S. officials reportedly urging Gulf allies to prepare for possible new strikes. Ukraine negotiations are set to continue in Abu Dhabi next week. The piece also covers a surge of bomb threats on European flights and the release of a new book about Emmanuel Macron.
summary: With the midterms over, attention turns to Donald Trump's next move on Iran, as US officials reportedly warn Gulf allies to prepare for new strikes. Ukraine talks head to Abu Dhabi next week.
author: Euronews

title: Thousands protest Paraguay banking scandal, demand impeachment of President Santiago Peña
content: Thousands of Paraguayans took to the streets to protest a banking scandal that has left nearly half the population unable to access their savings. Demonstrators are calling for President Santiago Peña to be impeached, even though he has offered to resign.
summary: Thousands of Paraguayans have taken to the streets over a banking scandal that left nearly half the population without access to their savings. Protesters are demanding President Santiago Peña face impeachment despite his offer to resign.
author: Euronews

title: Grizzly bear hunt launched after mother and daughter killed near Bella Coola, B.C.
content: A mother and her daughter were found dead after a suspected bear attack near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Conservation officers say several grizzlies may have been involved and are currently trapping the animals. Authorities have imposed a curfew while the investigation continues.
summary: A mother and her daughter were found dead after a suspected bear attack near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Conservation officers say multiple grizzlies may be involved, have started trapping, and authorities have imposed a curfew as the investigation continues.
author: Euronews

title: Iranian lawmaker Mottaki says IRGC disabling ships in Hormuz, urges US to lift blockade
content: Manouchehr Mottaki, an MP and former foreign minister under Ahmadinejad, told Euronews that the IRGC Navy was disabling multiple ships daily to eliminate unauthorized transit. He urged Washington to lift its naval blockade, which he said strangles the Iranian economy, before talks resume.
summary: MP and former foreign minister Manouchehr Mottaki said the IRGC Navy was disabling multiple ships each day to bring unauthorised transit through the Hormuz Strait to zero. He called on Washington to lift its naval blockade that he said is strangling the Iranian economy before talks resume.
author: Euronews

title: Two goats hired to clear vegetation at Yotsuya station draw crowds of commuters
content: In central Tokyo, two white goats have become unlikely celebrities after being recruited to clear overgrown vegetation near Yotsuya railway station. Commuters flock to see them grazing, and their eco‑friendly gardening duties attract crowds of delighted onlookers.
summary: Two white goats were recruited to clear overgrown vegetation near Yotsuya railway station in central Tokyo. Their eco‑friendly gardening duties have made them unlikely celebrities and attracted crowds of delighted onlookers.
author: Euronews

title: Deadly southern Ethiopia clashes force tens of thousands into Kenya
content: Deadly clashes between armed forces in southern Ethiopia have forced tens of thousands to flee into neighboring Kenya, with no clear timeline for their safe return. Ethiopia, Africa’s second‑most populous country with about 130 million people, is contending with multiple armed conflicts, especially along state borders.
summary: Deadly clashes between armed forces in southern Ethiopia have forced tens of thousands of people to flee into neighboring Kenya. The displaced have no idea when they can safely return home, while Ethiopia, Africa's second most populous country with around 130 million people, continues to grapple with multiple armed conflicts along its state borders.
author: France 24

title: Nigerian court invalidates Atiku Abubakar's African Democratic Congress presidential nomination
content:
A Nigerian court declared the nomination of Atiku Abubakar as the presidential candidate of the opposition African Democratic Congress invalid, ruling on Thursday just two months before the country’s elections.  

The party, which says the ruling All Progressives Congress was involved in the lawsuit, said it would appeal the decision.  Its spokesman noted that the ruling creates legal headaches for Abubakar and adds uncertainty for voters ahead of the January 16 vote.
summary: A Nigerian court on Thursday declared the nomination of Atiku Abubakar as the African Democratic Congress presidential candidate invalid. The party said it will appeal, accusing the ruling All Progressives Congress of involvement, and the ruling creates legal headaches for Abubakar and uncertainty for voters ahead of the January 16 election.
author: France 24

title: Death toll reaches 50 after Russian bombing of aid distribution point in Zaporizhzhia
content: Kyiv’s Emergency Service reported on Friday that the death toll from Russia’s bombing of an aid‑distribution point in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region has risen to 50. The strike, which occurred on Monday, is described as one of the deadliest attacks on civilians this year.
summary: Kyiv's Emergency Service said the death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region rose to 50. The strike, which occurred on Monday, is among the deadliest attacks on civilians this year.
author: France 24

title: Karachi residents block major roads over power cuts
content: Residents of Karachi, Pakistan’s economic hub, staged street blockades in recent days after enduring prolonged power cuts. The protests, which saw several major roads closed, underscore the city’s daily challenges. Karachi, a megacity of over 21 million people, has again been ranked among the world’s least livable cities.
summary: Residents of Karachi, Pakistan's economic hub, blocked several major roads in recent days after hours of power cuts. The protest highlights the daily problems—including pollution, shortages and crime—that affect the over‑21‑million‑person megacity, which has been ranked among the world’s least liveable cities.
author: France 24

title: School bus crash south of Bourg-en-Bresse kills at least two, injures 16
content: A school bus carrying 43 passengers crashed south of Bourg‑en‑Bresse in eastern France on Friday. The accident resulted in at least two deaths and 16 injuries among those on board.
summary: A bus carrying school children crashed south of Bourg-en-Bresse in eastern France on Friday, killing at least two people. The accident injured 16 others and the vehicle was carrying 43 passengers in total.
author: France 24

title: Republicans confront reckoning after Democrats' sweeping midterm win
content: Following the Democrats' sweeping victory in Tuesday's US midterm elections, Republicans are facing a moment of reckoning. With Donald Trump now a "lame-duck" president, the party must find a way forward after a historic electoral setback. The GOP faces major questions about how to win back voters and who will lead the party, with the next presidential election just two years away.
summary: Following the Democrats' sweeping victory in Tuesday's US midterm elections, Republicans are facing a moment of reckoning. With Donald Trump now a "lame-duck" president, the party must find a way forward after a historic electoral setback.
author: France 24

title: Israeli President Isaac Herzog to name government‑forming candidate on Sunday
content: Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced that on Sunday, Nov. 8, he will name the politician he will task with attempting to form a new government after meeting with all party leaders. In the preceding parliamentary vote, 46 members backed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, 67 supported his rival Gadi Eisenkot, and seven lawmakers abstained.
summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday, November 8, who he will task with trying to form a new government. In the parliamentary vote, 46 members recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, 67 backed Gadi Eisenkot, and seven lawmakers abstained.
author: France 24

title: Democrats face crowded, divided 2028 White House primary after midterm wins
content:
The United States midterm elections have concluded, and Democrats are now focusing on the 2028 presidential primary, which the source describes as potentially one of the most crowded and unpredictable in decades. Party leaders anticipate that the upcoming contest could highlight internal disagreements about the strategy needed to reclaim the White House.

Even after what the source calls “resounding victories on Tuesday,” Democrats remain split on whether to maintain a centrist approach or shift further left on issues such as healthcare, taxes, policing and foreign policy.
summary: Democrats are gearing up for a potentially crowded and unpredictable 2028 presidential primary that may expose internal party divisions. Despite strong Tuesday midterm victories, they remain split on whether to stay centrist or move further left on issues such as healthcare, taxes, policing and foreign policy.
author: France 24

title: Week of bomb threats and cyber‑attacks disrupt flights and fridges across Europe
content:
A series of disruptive incidents this week highlighted the fragility of modern life. Passenger flights across Europe were diverted after a multiplicity of hoax bomb threats, while a cyber‑attack targeted supermarket refrigerators in Belgium, Sweden and the United Kingdom and, in a further escalation, the cold‑storage facilities of France’s national blood service. The actors behind these disruptions have not been identified, and the events were described as occurring in a “grey zone” where the line between peace and conflict is increasingly blurred.

In the United Kingdom, comedian Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over a five‑year period. In the United States, former President Donald Trump signed a proclamation declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet Room national monuments that he says should be preserved from alteration by future administrations. Meanwhile, UK Labour leader Andy Burnham said he wants to “recast” the United Kingdom’s agreement to cede control of the Chagos Islands after resistance from Washington.

Health officials reported that cancer diagnoses in England have reached a record high, with more than 1,000 people diagnosed each day, according to NHS figures.

The United Nations‑recognised government of Yemen announced a reshuffle of its political and military leadership in an effort to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September.
summary: Hoax bomb threats diverted passenger flights across Europe and a cyber‑attack targeted supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden, the UK and France’s national blood service cold storage. The perpetrators have not been identified, and the incidents occur amid deepening global conflicts and a growing sense of vulnerability.
author: Guardian World

title: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
content: Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law. The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”.
summary: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted.
author: Guardian World

title: Europe places skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats force 35 plane searches
content: European authorities reported that hoax bomb threats against commercial flights this week have prompted heightened security measures across the continent. The incidents have led to at least 35 aircraft being searched or diverted. According to a statement from the French prime minister’s office, four additional threats targeting flights over French territory were received today. All affected planes landed safely, and bomb‑disposal units are conducting inspections while a probe seeks to identify the source of the threats affecting Europe.
summary: Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week, leading to searches or diversions of at least 35 planes. The French PM’s office said four new threats against aircraft over French territory were received, all planes landed safely, bomb dispersal units are inspecting them, and a probe is under way to determine the threats’ origin.

title: Experts say Australia faces same voter issues that flipped US Congress to Democrats
content:
Experts say Australia is confronting the same concerns that helped flip control of the U.S. Congress in the recent midterms.  Anthony Albanese’s government has already taken a blow from the Iran war, while voter anxiety about the cost of living and the development of datacentres could prove even more significant.

Observers note that the Democrats’ “stunning” midterm victory may broaden Australia’s alliance with the United States, as a new power base in Washington influences AUKUS, datacentre projects and relations with China.  Cabinet ministers, diplomats and the defence‑industrial sector closely watched the results, which saw congressional control shift to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years described as “badly dinted.”
summary: Experts say Australia is confronting voter concerns such as cost of living and datacentre development that helped the Democrats flip control of the US Congress in the recent midterms. The Albanese government also took a blow from the Iran war while officials watch implications for the Australia‑US alliance, AUKUS and relations with China.

title: Parliamentary inquiry says death possible in collision running and face‑slap contests
content: Impacts in emerging contact sports are akin to coward punches and cannot be made safer with regulation, neurologist says Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast Collision running and face-slapping competitions have similar impacts to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, with death a “distinct possibility”, a concussion expert has told a parliamentary inquiry. A New South Wales inquiry is examining whether emerging competitions such as Run Nation, in which two players run at each other and collide at high speed, and Power Slap, where players take turns slapping each other across the face, should be considered combat sports to better regulate the safety of participants.
summary: A New South Wales inquiry is examining whether emerging competitions such as Run Nation and Power Slap should be classified as combat sports to improve safety regulation. A neurologist told the inquiry that impacts in those contests are akin to coward punches, that death is a distinct possibility, and that regulation cannot make them safer.

title: Global stocks tumble as AI slowdown fears follow Democrats' midterm win
content:
Global equity markets fell sharply after a sell‑off on Wall Street on Thursday, with the decline spreading to Asian markets on Friday morning. The rout in U.S. technology stocks extended across the Atlantic, prompting European exchanges to tumble sharply. In London, the FTSE 100 dropped 1.9%, positioning the market for its worst day since March.

The downturn followed the Democrats’ midterm victory, which sparked investor concerns that the win could slow momentum in the artificial‑intelligence sector. The combined pressure from U.S., Asian and European markets underscored heightened fears of an AI slowdown.
summary: European stock markets fell sharply, with the FTSE down 1.9%, after a US tech sell‑off sparked by the Democrats’ midterm victory raised fears of an AI slowdown. The decline spread to Asian markets on Friday and left London poised for its worst day since March.

title: Midwest low pressure brings unseasonably warm November weather to New York, Boston
content:
An area of low pressure moving across the U.S. Midwest has drawn unusually warm air from the Gulf of Mexico into the eastern United States. The resulting temperatures reached about 23 °C (73 °F) in New York and Boston, roughly 7‑10 °C above typical early‑November values, and exceeded 20 °C in parts of eastern Canada, about 10‑15 °C above normal.

Meteorologists expect the low‑pressure system to drift eastward, after which temperatures should return closer to seasonal averages. Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms farther south have produced numerous flood and evacuation warnings across several states. The storms disrupted midterm‑day voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado, and a tornado that touched down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forced a polling station to be relocated. The tornado caused extensive damage but no casualties. State officials have asked for federal funding assistance to address the widespread damage to homes and infrastructure caused by the extreme weather.
summary: Midwest low pressure brings unseasonably warm November weather to New York, Boston.

title: ISS astronauts install final iROSA solar panel to augment aging power systems
content:
Astronauts Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency completed the installation of the final set of iROSA solar panels on the International Space Station (ISS) during EVA-101 on Thursday, Nov. 5. This spacewalk marked the conclusion of a critical power upgrade that had been ongoing since June 2021. The initiative was approved by NASA to address the degradation of the Station’s original solar panels, which were launched aboard Space Shuttle flights between 2000 and 2009. While six iROSA units were initially planned and installed between 2021 and 2023, additional power projections necessitated the procurement of two more units from Redwire for the 2A and 3B power channels on the ISS truss.

The last two iROSA units arrived on Cargo Dragon C211, which docked to the Harmony node module on Oct. 15 as part of the CRS-35 mission. Menon and Kutryk installed the first of these new units on the 2A channel during EVA-100 on Oct. 29. That spacewalk, which lasted seven hours and 11 minutes, was the 100th U.S. Segment EVA at the ISS without the Shuttle. During that mission, the astronauts deployed the array to its full length of 18.3 meters and connected the electrical system during orbital night to prevent electric shock.

EVA-101 focused on installing the final iROSA unit on the 3B power channel at the S6 truss on the starboard side of the Station. The spacewalk began at 13:36 UTC and followed a similar progression to the previous mission, involving the removal of the array from storage and its installation on a modification kit added during EVA-96 in August. A key difference in this mission was the manual handoff of the iROSA unit between the astronaut on the Canadarm2 and the free-floating crewmember, as the robotic arm could not reach the worksite. The astronauts also inspected and resolved an issue where only half of the expected current was flowing through the 3B power channel.

The mission concluded at 20:35 UTC after six hours and 59 minutes, marking the 286th overall spacewalk for ISS assembly, maintenance, and upgrades. It was the sixth spacewalk for Expedition 75 and the ninth at the Station in 2026. Following the completion of the upgrade, the ISS is equipped with approximately 215 kilowatts of power, providing sufficient margin for normal operations and science until its planned end of life around 2030.

The successful deployment of the final panels means the Station now has adequate power capacity for its remaining operational years. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman recently discussed the possibility of operating the ISS longer than originally planned in an interview on NSF’s The Flame Trench, expressing a desire to avoid a gap before a commercial successor is ready. The exact date for the Station’s disposal at Point Nemo in the Pacific remains under consideration. Menon now has a total of 33 hours and 30 minutes of EVA time, while Kutryk has accumulated 14 hours and 10 minutes.
summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed the installation of the final iROSA solar panel on the 3B power channel during US EVA-101. This upgrade ensures the International Space Station has sufficient power margin for operations and science until its planned end of life around 2030.

title: Como thrash Lens 9-1 in Bigger Cup clash
content:
Como delivered a dominant performance against Lens, securing a 9-1 victory in a match described as a display of outright vulgarity. The result was particularly notable given the ongoing criticism that the club is not sufficiently "Italian" to be a bona fide Serie A team. This perception is reinforced by the club’s ownership, which is bankrolled by an Indonesian cigarette manufacturer, and its president’s comparison of the multi-hubbed business model to that of the Walt Disney Company.

The team’s composition further fueled these traditionalist critiques, as Como was managed by Spanish coach Cesc Fàbregas. Their starting lineup against Lens did not include a single Italian player. The overwhelming nature of the win, which involved piling on goals against already-humiliated opponents, is noted as contrary to the typical Italian approach, unless both teams had formally agreed to such a scenario before the match began.
summary: Como defeated Lens 9-1 in a Bigger Cup match on Wednesday. The starting lineup featured no Italian players.

title: Scott Parker loses voice after dramatic West Ham return
content: The former midfielder with impressive managerial promotion record began with a thrilling comeback in draw at Cardiff Three days in and Scott Parker has already lost his voice. West Ham’s head coach arrived on Tuesday, watched his side fight back from 3-0 down to draw with Cardiff on Wednesday and was struggling to make himself heard when he met the media on Thursday afternoon. “It’s like in the summer holidays,” Parker said. “You put the flip-flops on for five weeks, then you come back home and you get your shoes on. You’re in a minute, you’ve got a blister on the back of your heel. It’s the same with a throat. I’ve not shouted for a little while. All of a sudden there’s shouting and it’s a bit croaky.”
summary: Scott Parker lost his voice three days after becoming West Ham's head coach and watching the team draw with Cardiff. He compared his hoarse throat to getting a blister after a long period of inactivity.

title: Golden State Valkyries celebrate first WNBA title with Bay Area parade
content: The Golden State Valkyries celebrated their first WNBA championship with a parade through San Francisco and Oakland. The team clinched the title in only their second season, marking a historic triumph for the franchise.
summary: The Golden State Valkyries held a parade through San Francisco and Oakland four days after winning their first WNBA championship. This historic triumph came in the team's second season, following a Game 7 victory led by Williams.

title: David Miller obituary: sports journalist and leading football and Olympics expert
content:
David Miller, a sports journalist recognized as a leading authority on football and the Olympics, has passed away. His career in regular sports journalism concluded in 2012, marking the end of decades of coverage for major international sporting events. Miller began his professional journey in 1956 as a junior staff member on the sports desk at the Times, shortly after graduating from Cambridge with a science degree.

Two years after joining the paper, Miller traveled to the 1958 football World Cup in Sweden on limited funds. He covered less prominent matches for six guineas per game. Over the course of his career, Miller observed 25 Summer and Winter Olympic Games, 14 Fifa World Cups, 62 FA Cup finals, 450 England football internationals, and 53 Wimbledon championships. He was widely acknowledged as one of the world’s leading experts in the fields of football and the Olympics.
summary: David Miller was a sports journalist who became a leading authority on football and the Olympics after starting at the Times in 1956. By 2012, he had covered 25 Olympic Games, 14 World Cups, and 450 England internationals.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Sydney Swans Engage External Advisers to Review Club Culture
content:
The Sydney Swans have hired external advisers to review the club’s culture following recent off-season incidents. These events include an August Melbourne hotel incident that resulted in the suspension of five players and Tom Papley’s alleged positive roadside drug test this week.

Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich expressed that the club is “bitterly disappointed” in Papley, one of the team’s most experienced players. Pavlich stated on Thursday that the club is disappointed to be dragged into another off-season scandal after Papley allegedly returned a positive result for methylamphetamine when stopped by police on Monday morning.
summary: The Sydney Swans have hired external advisers to review the club's culture following recent off-season incidents. CEO Matthew Pavlich expressed disappointment after Tom Papley allegedly tested positive for methylamphetamine.

title: Europa League: Dinamo Zagreb beat Sunderland 2-0 at Stadium of Light
content:
Sunderender’s unbeaten run in the Europa League ended with a 2-0 home defeat to Dinamo Zagreb at the Stadium of Light. Dinamo took the lead through a fierce strike by Luka Stojkovic, who also provided the assist for Dion Drena Beljo to double their advantage before halftime.

In other matches, Bournemouth secured a 3-1 victory at Sparta Prague with a goal from Evanilson. Meanwhile, Ferencvaros defeated Milan 2-0, maintaining their 100% record in the competition.
summary: Sunderland's unbeaten run in the Europa League ended with a 2-0 home defeat to Dinamo Zagreb. Luka Stojkovic scored the first goal and assisted Dion Drena Beljo for the second before halftime.

title: Sports owners lose political bet as Democrats sweep US elections
content:
Pro sports owners invested over $100 million in the recent election cycle, according to Front Office Sports, yet the Democratic sweep has altered Washington’s balance of power. The article describes Tuesday night as a referendum on both Donald Trump and MAGA policies, as well as the sports owners who influence American politics. It notes that the people voted, resulting in a loss for the owners.

The piece argues that Democrats are not merely rescuers from MAGA policies but are also integral to the system that enriches billionaire sports owners. It highlights that Democratic governors have been key partners in expanding legal sports betting. New Jersey Governor Phil Murphy placed the state’s first legal sports bet in 2018, while Illinois Governor JB Pritzker signed sports betting into law a year later. Additionally, New York’s mobile sportsbooks launched in 2022 under Governor Kathy Hochul, with the state retaining 51% of the revenue. Pritzker and Hochul both won re-election on Tuesday, demonstrating that in major betting markets, Democratic statehouses have been reliable partners for bookmakers.
summary: Pro sports owners invested over $100m in the election cycle, but voters rejected the Republican candidates they supported. Democratic governors in New Jersey, Illinois, and New York have previously enacted sports betting laws that significantly benefit the industry.
author: Guardian Sport

title: McIlroy gets two-shot penalty for improving lie at Abu Dhabi Championship
content: Rory McIlroy received a two-shot penalty for improving his lie during the opening round of the Abu Dhabi Championship. Jon Rahm also made a strong start in the same event.

title: Amanda McKinney projected to win Washington's 4th Congressional District
content:
Amanda McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, is projected to win Washington’s 4th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ.  

She defeated Air Force veteran John Duresky (D) in the race for the seat, which covers a large portion of the eastern half of the Evergreen State, an area that is more rural.

title: Meta, TikTok, Google sue California over child online safety law
content: Meta, TikTok, and Google have filed separate lawsuits against California, arguing that the state’s new “Digital Age Assurance Act” violates their First Amendment rights. The bipartisan legislation, which takes effect on January 1, prohibits social media platforms in the state from providing addictive services to children.
summary: Meta, TikTok, and Google filed separate lawsuits against California, arguing that the new legislation violates their First Amendment rights. The state's "Digital Age Assurance Act," which takes effect on January 1, bans social media platforms from providing addictive services to children.

title: Top Democrat vows ‘vigorous’ oversight of Pentagon
content: Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, pledged on Wednesday to conduct “vigorous” oversight of the Pentagon. Smith stated that this effort would include seeking testimonies from senior officials.

title: Democrat Jessica Killin flips longtime GOP-held Colorado House seat
content: Democrat Jessica Killin is projected to unseat Representative Jeff Crank in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ. This victory marks a political first for the Colorado Springs-area district, which has never elected a Democrat since its creation in 1973. Killin is an Army veteran who previously served as chief of staff.

title: Washington voters approve ban on transgender girls in school sports
content: Washington voters are projected to approve a ballot measure reversing the state’s long-standing policy allowing transgender girls to compete on girls’ and women’s school sports teams, according to Decision Desk HQ. The new measure requires students to submit healthcare provider documentation verifying their sex before participating on girls’ teams.
summary: Washington voters are projected to reverse a state policy allowing transgender girls to compete on girls’ school sports teams. The measure requires students to submit healthcare provider documentation verifying their sex before playing on a girls’ team.

title: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row
content: California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that he is commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor stated that the facility currently holds 548 people, which he described as the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row.

title: VR headsets lower presurgery anxiety and distress in children
content: A study by Dayanjan Wijesinghe of Virginia Commonwealth University, published in PLOS Digital Health, found that children using virtual reality headsets before surgery experienced reduced self-reported distress and fear. The research also noted lower heart rates and blood pressure in these patients.
summary: A study found that children using virtual reality before surgery reported less distress and fear. The participants also exhibited lower heart rates and blood pressure compared to those who did not use the technology.
author: Medical Xpress

title: COVID-19-related stress linked to faster epigenetic aging in adolescents
content: Researchers have linked COVID-19-related stress to faster epigenetic aging in adolescents, revealing biological consequences of the pandemic that had not previously been explored. While the pandemic and associated measures caused significant stress affecting physical and mental health across society, this study specifically identified impacts at the epigenetic level among young people. The findings have been published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic and its associated measures caused significant stress across all levels of society, negatively impacting physical and mental health. The biological consequences of this stress have not yet been explored.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study links indoor radon to higher heart failure risk in postmenopausal women
content: New research published in JAMA Network Open indicates that postmenopausal women residing in areas with higher estimated indoor radon levels may face an increased risk of heart failure. The study, led by researchers at the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health, provides the latest evidence suggesting that radon exposure could present a significant threat to the cardiac health of aging women.
summary: The study of postmenopausal women found that those living in areas with higher estimated indoor radon levels may have a higher risk of heart failure. The research was published in JAMA Network Open and was led by researchers at the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Karolinska Institutet and Mayo Clinic researchers publish review on early celiac disease stages
content:
As research into the interplay between genetics and environmental risk factors in early celiac disease expands, the need to harmonize scientific terms and concepts in the field has grown. In response, an effort led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and the Mayo Clinic has brought together 22 scientists from seven countries to address this challenge.

The collaborative team has published a review detailing the stages of early celiac disease. This paper, which aims to standardize terminology and concepts, has been published in the journal Gut.
summary: Researchers at Karolinska Institutet and the Mayo Clinic led a group of 22 scientists from seven countries to publish a review on the stages of early celiac disease. The paper, addressing the need to harmonize scientific terms and concepts, appears in the journal Gut.
author: Medical Xpress

title: I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
content: The article explores how negative job interview experiences can offer valuable insights into the professional world. It highlights that while these encounters are often unpleasant, they serve as learning opportunities for navigating the job market.

title: Employers Tighten Hybrid Rules as Employees Shift to Home Work
content: Office attendance from Monday to Friday was once a standard requirement for many jobs, but employees have increasingly developed a preference for working from home. In response to this shift, some employers have begun tightening their rules regarding hybrid work arrangements.
summary: Office attendance from Monday to Friday used to be a standard requirement for many jobs. Employees now prefer working from home, prompting some employers to tighten hybrid work rules.

title: Study links opaque Italian soccer club ownership to higher financial and criminal risks
content: The provided text poses questions regarding the ultimate ownership of Italian soccer clubs and the origins of their investment funds. It highlights the challenges in identifying individual controllers due to the use of investment funds, fiduciary companies, and transnational corporate structures. The content suggests that these opaque ownership arrangements are associated with higher financial and criminal risks.
